overview: Fletcher Building is New Zealand's largest vertically-integrated building materials, distribution and residential development group, dual-listed on the NZX and ASX (Foreign Exempt Listing). Following a multi-year strategic reset, the Group has simplified into a manufacturing- and distribution-led portfolio (Light Building Products, Heavy Building Materials, Distribution, Residential & Development) after selling its historically loss-making Construction division (including Higgins civil contracting) to VINCI Construction, completed 29 May 2026, and divesting smaller non-core units (Tradelink Australia, September 2024; Fletcher Reinforcing and Wire, April 2026). Core brands include GIB plasterboard, Laminex, PlaceMakers, Mico, Golden Bay Cement and Firth, with FY ending 30 June, operations concentrated in New Zealand, and a meaningful Australian manufacturing footprint (Laminex, Iplex, Stramit, Fletcher Insulation).

business_model.summary: Fletcher Building manufactures and distributes building materials (plasterboard, insulation, laminates, steel, concrete, aggregates, pipes) largely sold through its own and third-party merchant networks, supplemented by a residential land/home development business. Revenue is transactional and tied to construction and renovation activity rather than recurring/subscription in nature; earnings are highly geared to residential and commercial construction volumes in New Zealand and, to a lesser extent, Australia. The divested Construction division was project-based infrastructure/vertical building work that repeatedly generated large loss provisions (NZICC, Puhoi-Warkworth) and has now been fully exited; continuing-operations figures (FY2026 EBIT before Significant Items of $414m) represent the pure materials, distribution and residential business, with FY26 marking the first full-year net profit since FY23.

revenue_streams.name: Materials & Distribution (Light Building Products, Heavy Building Materials, Distribution)

business_model.customer_type: B2B trade/merchant and builder customers, plus B2C via retail-facing distribution (PlaceMakers, Mico) and direct residential home/land sales
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand ~75-80% of continuing revenue, Australia ~20-25% (Laminex, Iplex, Stramit, Fletcher Insulation); continuing-operations revenue was $5,644m in FY2025 (restated) and $2,866m in 1H FY26 (broadly flat vs $2,852m pcp)

main_competitors: James Hardie / USG Boral (plasterboard, fibre cement)
Holcim / Allied Concrete and cement importers (competing with Golden Bay/Firth)
Bunnings / Mitre 10 / ITM (merchant/distribution channel competing with PlaceMakers, Mico)
Marley, Vinidex, Aliaxis (pipes, competing with Iplex)
New plasterboard entrants (import-based competitors challenging GIB's historic dominance)
competitive_position.market_position: Dominant #1 position in NZ plasterboard (GIB/Winstone Wallboards, ~94% share per Commerce Commission), cement (Golden Bay) and building products distribution (PlaceMakers); smaller, more fragmented positions in Australia (Laminex, Iplex, Stramit)

moat_factors.description: ~94% NZ plasterboard market share (Winstone Wallboards) built over decades of manufacturing and code-compliance systems, though now under active regulatory and competitive challenge
PlaceMakers/Mico branch networks provide reach and trade relationships that are costly to replicate, though margins are thin and competitive
Ownership across aggregates-cement-concrete and manufacturing-distribution chains provides some cost and supply security advantages
GIB, Laminex and PlaceMakers are trusted, code-specified brands in NZ construction

weaknesses: Repeated history of value destruction from capital-heavy, low-return Construction/infrastructure contracting (now fully exited but legacy liabilities remain)

GIB's dominant position is a regulatory target: Commerce Commission Auckland High Court proceedings (filed Oct/Nov 2024) alleging retroactive rebate practices 2017-2022, with a trial date now set for 5 July 2027, and genuine new-entrant competition for the first time in decades
High fixed-cost manufacturing base is highly operationally geared to the NZ construction cycle, which remains subdued

Legacy quality/product liability issues (Iplex WA 'Pro-fit' pipes) reflect broader execution and quality-control weaknesses, with an unresolved Federal Court of Australia class action still heading to a lengthy (~12-week) trial
Balance sheet, while much improved, still constrains capital returns - no dividend has been paid since FY2023

growth_drivers: Cyclical recovery in NZ residential construction: building consents up materially YoY through FY2026, signalling an early-stage volume recovery feeding FY2027+ materials demand, though still below the ~51,000 2022 peak; management does not expect a 'meaningful' volume recovery until calendar 2027

Portfolio simplification into higher-return manufacturing/distribution segments (Construction sold to VINCI; Fletcher Reinforcing and Wire sold to United Industries) and adoption of ROIC as the central value metric, aimed at re-rating the business away from historically low group ROIC
Cost-out programme: ~$200m gross cost savings delivered through FY25, plus further FY26 savings in Warehouse/distribution and SG&A; head office headcount cut from 700+ to ~411

Balance sheet transformation: net debt cut from $1,766m (Jun-24) to $999m (Jun-25) to $637m (Jun-26), driven by the VINCI Construction sale proceeds and strong FY26 operating cash flow of $715m, opening the path to an eventual dividend policy reset once the Group achieves sustained positive free cash flow and net debt reaches the lower half of its target range

Growth capex in core manufacturing (new Firth Auckland batching plant, Fletcher Insulation Sonata Acoustics facility, recycled aggregate expansion at Winstone Aggregates) to support market share and efficiency as volumes recover
Early signs of stabilisation in the Australian manufacturing businesses (Laminex, Stramit) after a prolonged downturn

Decentralised operating model giving Business Unit General Managers full accountability for operational performance, customer relationships and ROIC, intended to sharpen capital discipline across the simplified portfolio

business.description: Group earnings are highly geared to NZ (and to a lesser extent Australian) residential, commercial and civil construction volumes; management flagged that macro uncertainty and rising input costs are delaying or cancelling new commercial projects, weighing on 1H FY27 performance even as residential slowly recovers
New entrants are challenging GIB's historic near-monopoly for the first time in decades, threatening the Group's highest-margin franchise

Even after divesting Construction to VINCI, Fletcher Building retains liabilities/risk on NZICC and other legacy vertical projects, including active SkyCity litigation over NZICC (NZICC reached Practical Completion and was handed over in Feb-2026), which the company says it will 'vigorously defend'

business.risk: Execution risk on new divisional structure
business.description: The 1 July 2025 reorganisation into Light Building Products/Heavy Building Materials/Distribution/Residential & Development, alongside the completed Construction exit and smaller divestments, is a major operating model change that delivered a positive FY26 result but remains early in its embedding

financial.risk: Earnings still cyclically depressed vs. mid-cycle potential
financial.description: FY2026 EBIT from continuing operations before Significant Items was $414m, well up YoY and a genuine inflection, but still below prior-cycle peak levels achieved when NZ residential/commercial volumes were stronger

financial.risk: Capital allocation constrained until net debt normalises further
financial.description: Net debt fell to $637m at Jun-2026 (from $999m at Jun-2025), inside the $400m-$900m target range, but no dividend has been declared since FY2023; the Board has said it will reset dividend policy only once the Group has sustained positive free cash flow and net debt is in the lower half of the target range
Meaningful Australian manufacturing revenue and costs create translation and transaction exposure

regulatory.risk: Commerce Commission proceedings against Winstone Wallboards (GIB)
regulatory.description: The Commerce Commission's Auckland High Court case (filed Oct/Nov 2024) alleges Winstone Wallboards' retroactive tiered rebate arrangements with merchants (2017-2022) breached the Commerce Act (sections 27 and 36); a trial date has now been set for 5 July 2027. Winstone (~94% NZ wallboard market share) is 'vigorously defending' and disputes the Commission's conclusions, but the case carries reputational, remedial and potential penalty risk over an extended timeline

regulatory.risk: Iplex Australia WA 'Pro-fit' pipes matter - unresolved class action
regulatory.description: Despite the ~A$155m (NZ$170m) Industry Response provision (finalised June 2025, WA Government funding 20%/Iplex 80%), a separate Federal Court of Australia class action (Baker McKenzie acting for claimants) alleging Typlex-resin Pro-fit pipes are prone to crazing/cracking is proceeding toward a lengthy (~12-week) trial in 2026/2027, with a related BGC claim also in train; potential for further provisioning beyond the Industry Response
Ongoing NZ government building consent and code reform could affect product specification requirements and competitive dynamics in plasterboard and other regulated materials

macro.description: Mortgage rates and the RBNZ OCR path directly drive housing starts/consents and therefore the Group's core materials volumes; any renewed tightening would be a fresh headwind to the still-fragile residential recovery
Below-average population growth and a large stock of unsold/available homes are cited as headwinds to new residential starts converting into completed, materials-consuming construction

Management specifically flagged that macro/geopolitical uncertainty and rising input costs are causing commercial projects to be delayed or cancelled, pressuring 1H FY27 performance even as residential slowly turns

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ residential building consents recovered through FY2026 from cyclical lows, signalling an early-stage volume recovery that should progressively flow into materials demand, though still well below the ~51,000 2022 peak; management guides to a more 'meaningful' recovery only from calendar 2027, with 1H FY27 pressured by soft commercial construction. Australian conditions show early signs of stabilisation but remain uneven.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - Fletcher Building is a classic late-cycle, capital-intensive building materials/distribution business with high operating leverage to residential and commercial construction activity; historically the Group has swung from peak EBIT of several hundred million dollars to statutory losses within a few years, reflecting large fixed manufacturing costs against volatile volumes
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - mortgage rates and the RBNZ OCR path directly drive housing starts/consents and therefore the Group's core materials volumes

recent_developments.event: Fletcher Building set its 2026 Annual Shareholders' Meeting for 21 October 2026 in Auckland; a substantial shareholder (Schroder Investment Management Australia) trimmed its stake from ~6.16% to ~5.13% in early September 2026

FY2026 full-year results released 19 August 2026: EBIT from continuing operations before Significant Items of $414m (up $85m YoY, within the raised $400m-$403m headline guidance range that included ~$52m of property sale gains); net earnings attributable to shareholders of $228m (vs. a $647m loss in FY25, restated for discontinued operations); EPS of 21.2 cents (vs. a 41.4-cent loss); operating cash flow of $715m (up from $501m); net debt reduced to $637m (from $999m at Jun-2025), inside the $400m-$900m target range. Shares rallied ~5.5% on the announcement. No FY26 dividend declared; Board to reset dividend policy once the Group has sustained positive free cash flow and net debt is in the lower half of the target range. Management flagged 1H FY27 will remain pressured by soft commercial construction and macro/geopolitical uncertainty, with a meaningful volume recovery not expected until calendar 2027

Fletcher Building raised FY26 continuing-operations EBIT before Significant Items guidance to $400m-$403m (including ~$52m from surplus property sales, notably the Laminex Cheltenham site); ex-property EBIT guided at $348m-$351m, ~3.6% above prior guidance midpoint, driven by stronger Light Building Materials procurement/productivity

Fletcher Building requested and secured withdrawal of its Moody's credit rating (effective 25 June 2026) after a string of asset sales reduced net debt, while continuing to target investment-grade balance sheet metrics

Sale of the Construction division (including Higgins civil contracting) to VINCI Construction completed on 29 May 2026, with the purchase price increased from $315.6m to ~$334m after Higgins signed additional Integrated Delivery Contracts; ~2,300 employees transferred with the division

Fletcher Building agreed to sell the smaller Fletcher Reinforcing and Wire business to United Industries for NZ$15.7m, flagging a loss on sale of up to NZ$23m, as part of continued portfolio simplification around ROIC

1H FY26 result: revenue from continuing operations $2,866m (broadly flat vs 1H FY25's $2,852m); EBIT from continuing operations before Significant Items of $145m; net earnings from continuing operations of $45m attributable to shareholders - the first positive continuing-operations half since June 2023; operating cash flow improved to $156m (vs $87m pcp); Construction division reclassified as a discontinued operation from 31 December 2025 pending divestment, resulting in a net loss attributable to shareholders of -$11m after -$56m of discontinued-operations losses; available liquidity ~$0.8bn plus a new $200m bank liquidity facility. NZICC reached Practical Completion and was handed over to SkyCity in February 2026; Fletcher Building retains legacy liabilities/risk on the project and states it will 'vigorously defend' SkyCity's related litigation

FY2025 result: statutory EBIT of -$260m (vs. +$384m before $644m of Significant Items); revenue down ~9% to $6,994m (continuing basis) / $7,196m total group; net loss attributable to shareholders of $419m; no FY25 dividend declared; A$155m (NZ$170m) Iplex Australia WA 'Pro-fit' pipes Industry Response provision finalised in June 2025

guidance.as_of: 19 August 2026 (FY2026 full-year results and FY2027 outlook commentary)

items.metric: FY2026 EBIT from continuing operations before Significant Items (actual, for reference)
items.notes: Up $85m YoY; includes property sale gains within the guided range; FY26 also delivered net earnings of $228m and operating cash flow of $715m

items.target: No specific point guidance issued; qualitative outlook only
items.notes: Management expects economic, political and geopolitical uncertainty to weigh on 1H FY27 performance, with commercial project delays/cancellations and residential volumes below prior year; a 'meaningful recovery in underlying volumes' is still not anticipated until calendar year 2027
Down from $999m at Jun-2025 and $1,766m at Jun-2024, driven by VINCI Construction sale proceeds and strong FY26 operating cash flow

items.target: No dividend; policy to be reset once sustained positive free cash flow achieved and net debt reaches lower half of $400m-$900m target range
items.notes: No dividend paid since FY2023; net debt improvement (to $637m) brings the Group closer to conditions for a policy reset, but management has not committed to a specific resumption date

items.target: Maintain cost discipline and capture upside when demand improves
items.notes: Follows ~$200m+ of gross cost savings delivered through the FY25-FY26 turnaround programme; head office headcount reduced from 700+ to ~411

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Andrew Reding said Fletcher Building is 'significantly more resilient than it was twelve months ago,' crediting the Construction divestment and balance sheet strengthening. Management continues to caution that the economic, political and geopolitical backdrop remains uncertain and is expected to weigh on 1H FY27 performance, with commercial projects being delayed or cancelled and residential volumes still below prior-year levels; a meaningful recovery in underlying volumes is not anticipated until calendar year 2027. Priorities for FY27 are maintaining cost discipline while positioning to capture upside once demand improves.

bull_case: Genuine, now largely completed self-help turnaround: Construction division (including chronic loss-makers Higgins/NZICC-style vertical projects) fully divested to VINCI, non-core units exited, $200m+ of structural cost-out delivered, and ROIC embedded as the central internal value metric - FY26 delivered the first full-year net profit ($228m) since FY23

Balance sheet transformed - net debt down from $1,766m (Jun-24) to $637m (Jun-26), operating cash flow up to $715m in FY26, Moody's rating voluntarily withdrawn from a position of strength, and the Group now sits comfortably within its $400m-$900m target range, opening a credible path to dividend policy reset

Dominant NZ market positions (GIB plasterboard ~94% share, Golden Bay cement, PlaceMakers distribution) retain strong operating leverage to any recovery; NZ residential consents have been recovering off cyclical lows through FY2026, a tailwind for FY2027-28 materials volumes as a structural housing shortage persists

Simplified, decentralised portfolio (Light Building Products, Heavy Building Materials, Distribution, Residential & Development) is easier for the market to understand and value than the old conglomerate structure, reducing the 'execution risk discount' that has weighed on the stock for years

Shares have re-rated materially off their 2025 lows (roughly $2.65 to ~$3.71+) but a dividend resumption, once conditions are met, would likely be a further re-rating catalyst for income-oriented NZX investors
bear_case: Structurally low historical returns and a long history of value destruction (NZICC, Puhoi-Warkworth, Iplex WA pipes, multiple divisional impairments) mean legacy liabilities are still retained even after the Construction exit - active SkyCity NZICC litigation and an unresolved, ~12-week Federal Court Iplex class action trial both carry open-ended financial and reputational risk

Management itself does not expect a 'meaningful' volume recovery until calendar 2027, and has explicitly flagged that macro/geopolitical uncertainty and rising input costs are causing commercial projects to be delayed or cancelled, pressuring 1H FY27 even as the FY26 turnaround narrative plays out

GIB's historically dominant, high-margin plasterboard franchise (~94% NZ share) faces a Commerce Commission Auckland High Court case (trial now set for 5 July 2027) alleging anti-competitive rebate conduct, plus genuine new-entrant competition for the first time in decades - a structural, multi-year overhang on the Group's best asset

No dividend has been paid since FY2023 and management has still not committed to a resumption date, capping near-term shareholder returns despite the improved balance sheet; analyst consensus rating is a 'Hold' with price targets clustered around/below the current share price

The stock has already re-rated substantially off its 2025 lows and is trading near recent highs; with much of the self-help/deleveraging story now reflected in FY26 results, further upside likely requires the cyclical volume recovery to actually materialise on schedule, leaving limited margin of safety if calendar-2027 recovery disappoints or slips further
